claims.text: Sustained loading of nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings induces progressive plastic deformation controlled by heterogeneous interfaces.
Dislocations preferentially accumulate at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Lattice mismatch and severe local distortion cause preferential dislocation accumulation at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Once a critical interfacial dislocation density is reached, intermittent interface sliding and dislocation transmission occur.
Intermittent interface sliding and dislocation transmission allow strain relaxation.
The proposed starting material is an alternating nanoscale FCC/BCC HEA multilayer with minimal interdiffusion and a stable phase distribution.
The creep test is to be conducted below temperatures that induce phase changes while still activating dislocation movement.
Layer thickness below 100 nm is proposed as the nanoscale regime for the comparison.
Moderate temperatures can provide a regime in which dislocation climb and interface sliding are active without unwanted diffusion or phase transformation.
FCC/BCC interfaces act as barriers to dislocation motion and as sites for dislocation pile-up.
Severe lattice distortion and compositional complexity, together with interfacial mismatch, create local stress concentrations.
Local stress concentrations promote dislocation pile-up at the interfaces.
Increasing interfacial dislocation density eventually produces sufficient accumulated stress for intermittent interface sliding or dislocation climb.
Homogeneous HEA films distribute dislocations more evenly and lack comparable interface-mediated deformation events.
Under sustained loading, the multilayer coatings will have a slower but progressively accelerating strain rate relative to homogeneous films.
TEM will reveal higher dislocation densities localized at multilayer boundaries.
TEM will reveal signs of interface sliding localized at multilayer boundaries.
Creep curves will contain sudden strain-relaxation milestones corresponding to episodes of interface activation.
Interdiffusion, phase transformation, or excessive layer thickening can change the proposed deformation mechanism.
Failure to observe enhanced interfacial dislocation density, interface sliding, or a creep-rate difference from the homogeneous control would falsify the proposed interface-controlled mechanism.
